```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(pdmS7)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  error = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 3.8, dpi = if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"))) 110 else 60
)
pal <- c("#444444", "#236b83", "#a26421", "#5b8c3a", "#8a3b6b", "#b23b3b", "#9aa7b0")
old <- options(pdmS7.user = "Ann Custodian", pdmS7.role = "custodian")
f1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
f0 <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f", x)
```

A model calibrated on a river's record is fitted to the floods in that record. It is used for
the floods that are not: the ones that matter most. A calibration can score well on every
window and still go wrong once flows pass anything it was fitted to. Three things cause most
of the trouble.

- **Large floods are rare.** The parameters that control them, chiefly the soil store's
  capacity and the fast routing, are barely tested by the record. Many settings fit it
  equally well and then disagree above it.
- **The optimiser uses every freedom it has.** A store that only fills in a big flood costs
  nothing to get wrong if no big flood occurs during calibration, so its fitted value is
  close to arbitrary.
- **The largest observed flows are themselves extrapolated.** Above the highest flow ever
  gauged, the rating curve is a line drawn beyond its data. The size of those flows is
  uncertain, even though their order is not.

No calibration method removes these. pdmS7 makes them visible, in the record, before anyone
signs off.

# What pdmS7 does

| Check | How | When |
|---|---|---|
| **Wettest years held back** | The two wettest water years (October to September) in the calibration and validation windows, ranked by their highest flow, are left out of every calibration, trial and validation score. | Chosen at registration; scored once, with the test |
| **Spread of equally good fits** | Each automatic calibration keeps the parameter sets it tried that score within a tolerance of its best (0.02 NSE by default), up to 50 spread-out sets. The test runs every one through the held-back years. | Kept at calibration; reported at the test |
| **Rating flag** | Given the highest gauged flow, registration counts the flows above it in each window, and the test marks each held-back peak that lies above it. | Recorded at registration and test |

Holding back the largest floods is the differential split-sample test of Klemeš (1986): fit on
one kind of conditions, test on another. Ranking years by their highest flow survives rating
error, because a rating rises with stage: it may get a flood's size wrong, but not whether it
was bigger than another. The rating flag does not change the fit. It tells the reviewer where
the observed numbers deserve less trust.

# The example

Ten water years of daily data from a made-up 60 km2 catchment. Two storms, in 2013-14 and
2018-19, are far larger than anything else in the record. The model's soil store holds up to
250 mm, and only those two storms come close to filling it. The observations carry 5 per cent
noise.

```{r data}
set.seed(21)
n <- 365 * 10
time <- seq(as.POSIXct("2010-10-01", tz = "UTC"), by = 86400, length.out = n)
rain <- ifelse(runif(n) < 0.45, rgamma(n, 0.7, scale = 7), 0)
rain[c(1200, 1201, 2950, 2951, 2952)] <- c(70, 55, 60, 75, 40)
forcing <- data.frame(time = format(time, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"), rain = rain,
                      pet = 1.2 + sin(2 * pi * (seq_len(n) - 100) / 365))
truth <- pdm_presets("standard")
truth$dt <- 24
truth$area_km2 <- 60
truth$distribution$cmax <- 250
truth$surface$k1 <- 30
truth$fc <- 1.05
model <- pdm_from_config(truth)
observed <- run_pdm(model, forcing[, -1], initial_state_from_flow(model, 1.5, 0.7))$output$q_m3s *
  exp(rnorm(n, 0, 0.05))
years <- wettest_years(time, observed, n = 2)
years[, c("water_year", "start", "peak_m3s", "held")]
```

`wettest_years()` is what `register_data()` uses. The two held-back years have peaks of
`r f0(years$peak_m3s[1])` and `r f0(years$peak_m3s[2])` m3/s; no other year exceeds
`r f0(years$peak_m3s[3])`.

# Registering the data

Suppose the station's highest check gauging is 30 m3/s. Everything above that comes from an
extended rating.

```{r register}
project <- file.path(tempdir(), "wet-brook")
unlink(project, recursive = TRUE)
start_calibration_project(project, catchment = "Wet Brook", gauge = "00001",
                          purpose = "Flood forecasting", area_km2 = 60,
                          owner = "Area Manager", steward = "Sam Steward")
reg <- register_data(project, forcing, observed,
                     calibration = c("2011-01-01", "2016-09-30"),
                     validation = c("2016-10-01", "2019-09-30"),
                     test = c("2019-10-01", "2020-09-27"),
                     highest_gauged_m3s = 30,
                     reasoning = "Ten years; rating checked to 30 m3/s.")
check <- reg$rating_check$windows
data.frame(window = names(check), steps_above = sapply(check, `[[`, "steps_above"),
           highest_m3s = round(sapply(check, `[[`, "highest_m3s"), 1))
```

The rating check, recorded in the entry, shows the problem at once. Every flow above the
gauged limit lies in the held-back years. The highest flow left for calibration and
validation is `r f1(max(check$calibration$highest_m3s, check$validation$highest_m3s))` m3/s,
about half the limit. Without the hold-out, the calibration would have been fitted to
`r check$wettest$steps_above` days of extrapolated flow, and nothing in the record would have
said so.

# Calibrating

An ordinary automatic calibration of every parameter, from the standard starting point.

```{r calibrate}
start <- pdm_presets("standard")
start$dt <- 24
start$area_km2 <- 60
select_structure(project, start, "Standard structure.")
b <- calibration_bounds(start)
fit <- log_auto_calibration(
  project, parent = 3, lower = setNames(b$lower, b$path), upper = setNames(b$upper, b$path),
  log_scale = b$path[b$scale == "log"], starts = 3, seed = 2, control = list(maxit = 40),
  reasoning = "All parameters, three starts."
)
good <- fit$equally_good
c(nse = fit$scores$nse, trials_within_tolerance = good$within, sets_kept = length(good$sets))
```

The calibration NSE is `r sprintf("%.3f", fit$scores$nse)`. Of the parameter sets the search
tried, `r good$within` scored within 0.02 of the best; 50 spread-out ones are kept. How far
apart are they?

```{r spread-parameters}
sets <- do.call(rbind, lapply(good$sets, function(s) unlist(s$parameters)))
spread <- t(apply(sets, 2, range))
data.frame(truth = sapply(colnames(sets), function(p) pdmS7:::.path_get(truth, p)),
           lowest = signif(spread[, 1], 3), highest = signif(spread[, 2], 3))
```

```{r cmax, include=FALSE}
cmax <- range(sets[, "distribution.cmax"])
```

The soil capacity `cmax` spans `r f0(cmax[1])` to `r f0(cmax[2])` mm among fits that all
reproduce the calibration record almost equally well. The record cannot tell them apart,
because in those years the soil never comes near full. This is the arbitrary parameter the
introduction warned of, and it is exactly the one a large flood depends on.

# The test

Validation and the test follow the usual rules. The test also reveals the held-back years.

```{r test}
propose_candidate(project, fit$id, "Best automatic fit.")
validation <- validate_candidate(project, "Validation holds up.")
test <- test_candidate(project, "Final check, including the wettest years.")
c(validation = validation$validation_scores$nse, test_window = test$test_scores$nse,
  wettest_years = test$wettest$scores$nse)
peaks <- do.call(rbind, lapply(test$wettest$years, as.data.frame))
peaks[, -1] <- lapply(peaks[, -1], function(x) if (is.numeric(x)) round(x, 1) else x)
peaks
```

```{r peaks, include=FALSE}
miss <- 100 * (peaks$simulated_peak_m3s / peaks$observed_peak_m3s - 1)
width <- 100 * (peaks$spread_high_m3s - peaks$spread_low_m3s) / peaks$observed_peak_m3s
above <- peaks$observed_peak_m3s > peaks$spread_high_m3s
```

Every score looks fine, including over the wettest years, where NSE is dominated by the many
ordinary days. The peaks tell the real story.

- The candidate's peaks are `r f0(abs(miss[1]))` and `r f0(abs(miss[2]))` per cent
  `r if (all(miss < 0)) "low" else "off"`.
- The equally good sets span `r f0(width[1])` and `r f0(width[2])` per cent of the observed
  peak.
- In `r if (all(above)) "both years" else paste(peaks$water_year[above], collapse = " and ")`
  the observed peak lies above every one of them. The range
  shows how far fits the record cannot tell apart disagree. It is not a confidence interval,
  and the truth can lie outside it.
- Both observed peaks lie above the highest gauging, so on a real river even the "observed"
  values would be uncertain.

```{r hydrograph, fig.height=4.2}
y <- reg$scorecard$wettest$years[[1]]
peak <- y$first_row - 1 + which.max(observed[y$first_row:y$last_row])
rows <- (peak - 15):(peak + 45)
simulate <- function(parameters) {
  cfg <- fit$configuration
  for (p in names(parameters)) cfg <- pdmS7:::.path_set(cfg, p, parameters[[p]])
  m <- pdm_from_config(cfg)
  run_pdm(m, forcing[, -1], initial_state_from_flow(m, observed[1], 0.7))$output$q_m3s[rows]
}
ensemble <- sapply(good$sets, function(s) simulate(s$parameters))
candidate <- simulate(list())
plot(time[rows], observed[rows], type = "n", ylim = c(0, max(ensemble, observed[rows]) * 1.05),
     xlab = "", ylab = "Flow (m3/s)", main = paste("Largest flood, water year", y$water_year))
polygon(c(time[rows], rev(time[rows])), c(apply(ensemble, 1, min), rev(apply(ensemble, 1, max))),
        col = adjustcolor(pal[2], 0.25), border = NA)
abline(h = 30, lty = 2, col = pal[7])
lines(time[rows], candidate, col = pal[2], lwd = 2)
points(time[rows], observed[rows], pch = 16, cex = 0.5, col = pal[1])
legend("topright", c("observed", "candidate", "equally good sets", "highest gauging"),
       col = c(pal[1], pal[2], adjustcolor(pal[2], 0.4), pal[7]), pch = c(16, NA, 15, NA),
       lty = c(NA, 1, NA, 2), lwd = c(NA, 2, NA, 1), bty = "n")
```

# Reading the result

The scores answer "does the model reproduce this river?". The held-back peaks answer the
question a forecaster asks: "would it have got the big one right?". Read the table in three
parts.

- **The candidate against the observed peak.** A large miss on floods the model never saw is
  the plainest sign that the calibration does not extrapolate.
- **The width of the range.** A wide range means the record cannot pin down the parameters
  that control large floods. The candidate's own peak is then partly luck, good or bad.
- **The rating flag.** Where the observed peak lies above the highest gauging, a miss may be
  the rating's error rather than the model's. Treat both as uncertain.

When the range is wide, more calibration effort will not help. The remedies change what the
calibration knows: fix the poorly constrained parameter from independent evidence (soil
data for `cmax`, say), choose a simpler structure that extrapolates predictably (see
[Choosing a model structure](choosing-structure.html)), or extend the rating with new
gaugings. Record the decision, with its reasons, in a note before sign-off.

# Settings

| Argument of `register_data()` | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `wettest_years` | 2 | Years held back. Needs a `time` column and enough record to leave three years. 0 holds none back. |
| `highest_gauged_m3s` | none | The top of the reliable rating. Flows above it are flagged, never changed. |
| `tie_tolerance` | 0.02 | How close to the best calibration score, in the headline's units, a set must be to count as equally good. |

The test needs both the held-back years and a logged automatic calibration to report a
range. A manual trial, or a fit from a structure comparison, keeps no record of the
alternatives, so its range is the candidate alone, and the report says so. Projects registered before version 0.5.0 hold nothing back.

# Reference

Klemeš, V. (1986) Operational testing of hydrological simulation models. *Hydrological
Sciences Journal* 31(1), 13-24.
